opus-5.5.text:
I think a few things have come together at the same time, and that's why it feels like we're at an inflection point.

The first is that the base models have finally become good enough at reasoning. For a long time, language models were very good at imitating text, but when you put them in an environment, a website, a codebase, a computer, they would get lost after a few steps. What changed is that we learned how to make models *think* before acting, to use language as a kind of internal tool for reasoning. Once a model can reason, plan, and reflect on its mistakes, it can generalize to new environments it has never seen. That's the key difference between the old generation of agents, like the reinforcement learning agents that played Go or Atari, and today's agents. The old ones were superhuman in one narrow environment. The new ones are maybe not superhuman anywhere yet, but they can work across many environments.

The second thing is that the recipe for training has started to work. Pre-training gives you a strong prior about the world, and reinforcement learning on top of that, with reasoning in the loop, actually generalizes. A few years ago, RL was something you did in a game. Now you can do RL on math, on coding, on real tasks, and the improvement transfers. So we have both the prior and the method.

The third thing, which I think people underestimate, is the shift in where the bottleneck is. I sometimes describe it as moving into the "second half" of AI. In the first half, the main game was inventing new methods and models and beating benchmarks. Now the methods are general enough that the bottleneck becomes: what problems are we actually defining? How do we evaluate real-world utility? Once you start building environments and evaluations that look like real work, like customer service, software engineering, or operating a computer, you very quickly find out what's missing and you can close the gap. That loop is much faster than before.

And finally, there's the product and infrastructure side. Coding agents are a good example. Developers are already using them every day, which produces feedback, which produces better models. Once an agent creates real value in one domain, the economic pull is enormous, and that money and attention flows back into making the next domain work.

So my expectation is not that one day there's a single magical agent that does everything. It's more that, domain by domain, agents will cross the threshold from "interesting demo" to "actually useful," and because the underlying capability is general, that crossing will happen faster and faster. From the outside, that will look like an explosion.

r001.rationale: The response says the training recipe and reasoning capabilities have improved, but it does not state that a general method for building AI agents became available around 2024–2025.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that the hard part is finally done, and what's left is mostly engineering and products.

For a long time, "agent" was a word people used loosely. If you go back to my time at Princeton, when we did ReAct and later SWE-agent, the models themselves were the bottleneck. You could design a beautiful loop, thinking, acting, observing, but if the model couldn't reason across a few steps or recover from a mistake, the whole thing collapsed. Most demos worked once and then fell apart on the second try.

What changed is that reasoning became something you can train directly. Once you have reinforcement learning on top of a strong base model, the model learns not just to answer, but to try, fail, reflect, and try again. That is exactly the behavior an agent needs. So the capability that was missing for ten years showed up more or less in the last two.

The second reason is that the environments are now there. Agents learn from feedback, and the places that give clean feedback, code, terminals, browsers, APIs, are also the places where the economic value is concentrated. Software engineering is the obvious example. You can run tests, you can see whether the thing worked. That makes it a perfect training ground, and also a product that people pay for immediately. I think we'll see this pattern repeat in domain after domain, wherever you can define what "done" looks like.

And the third thing, honestly, is that we've moved into what I'd call the second half. The first half was about building better methods and beating benchmarks. The second half is about defining the right problems and the right evaluations. When you measure agents on long-horizon, real-world tasks instead of single questions, you start optimizing for the thing that actually matters, and progress compounds much faster.

So when people ask why I'm confident, it's not that I think one magic model is coming. It's that the ingredients, reasoning, tools, environments, and good evaluations, have all arrived at the same time. Historically, when that happens, the explosion isn't a question of if, it's a question of who builds it first.

r001.rationale: The response says agent-enabling reasoning became directly trainable and that this missing capability appeared in the last two years, placing its availability around 2024–2025.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re reaching a point where AI can move from answering questions to actually doing things. When you ask a chatbot a question, you still have to take its answer and carry out the work yourself. An agent can potentially take a goal, use tools, observe what happened, and decide what to do next. That makes a much larger range of tasks possible.

The challenge is reliability. A model can be impressive in a single interaction, but if a task requires twenty steps, small mistakes can accumulate. So the timing depends on models getting better at reasoning, using tools, and recovering when something goes wrong. The systems around the models also need to improve—how they get context, how we evaluate them, and when they ask a person for help.

I expect progress to compound because these pieces reinforce each other. Better models make useful agent applications possible; those applications reveal concrete failures, which give us better targets for improvement. And a lot of work already happens through digital interfaces, so there’s a large space where agents can become useful.

I don’t think that requires a fully autonomous agent that can do everything. It can start with a bounded task that an agent does well, with human supervision. If that becomes reliable and inexpensive enough, people will use it, and gradually delegate more.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents becoming practical and improving over time, but does not state that a general method for building them became available around 2024–2025.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that we’re moving from AI that answers questions to AI that actually does things. A chatbot can tell you how to solve a problem, but an agent can use tools, interact with an environment, see what happened, and decide what to do next. That opens up a much larger set of applications.

For that to work, several things have to come together. The model needs to be capable enough to reason through a task, the tools need to be accessible, and the system needs a way to recognize mistakes and recover. Those pieces are improving together. Many useful tasks already happen on computers, so an agent can start creating value without waiting for progress in robotics.

There’s also a feedback loop. Once agents can attempt real tasks, we can evaluate whether they succeeded and use that feedback to improve them. For some tasks, success is much more concrete than whether a chatbot’s answer sounds good: Did the code pass the tests? Did the requested operation actually happen?

I don’t think this means a completely autonomous assistant will suddenly handle everything. The first big wave will probably be in narrower settings, where the objective is clear and results are easy to check. But even within those boundaries, the amount of useful work is enormous. That’s why I expect rapid growth over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response discusses improving agent capabilities and expects rapid growth, but it does not state that a general method for building agents became available around 2024–2025.
